Graphql Introduction.exp: Introduction to graphql and its ecosystem.

Schema: A GraphQL schema defines the shape of available data and operations using the Schema Definition Language (SDL). It acts as a contract between client and server, specifying types, queries, and mutations.
Queries: Queries are read-only operations that request specific fields from the server. Clients specify exactly which fields they need, eliminating over- and under-fetching common in REST APIs.
Mutations: Mutations are write operations that create, update, or delete data. They follow the same field-selection pattern as queries but guarantee sequential execution and can return the modified state.

N+1 Problem: The N+1 problem occurs when resolving related fields triggers one query per parent item. DataLoader batches these into single queries, while inspecting query plans and using JOIN-based resolvers provide further optimization.
Security: GraphQL security involves query depth limiting, complexity analysis, rate limiting, authentication, authorization, and persistent whitelisted queries. These prevent malicious queries from overloading the server.
Pagination: Cursor-based pagination is the GraphQL standard using `after`/`before` with `first`/`last` arguments. It provides consistent results even when data changes, unlike offset-based pagination which can skip or duplicate items.

Scalars: GraphQL's built-in scalar types are Int, Float, String, Boolean, and ID. Custom scalars (Date, JSON, URL) can be defined for domain-specific data with custom validation and serialization logic.
Objects: Object types represent complex data structures with named fields, each returning a specific type. Fields can be required (`!`), have default values, and accept arguments for filtering or transformation.

type Product {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
  description: String
  price: Float!
  inStock: Boolean!
  categories: [Category!]!
  reviews: [Review!]!
  createdAt: String!
}

type Category {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
  products: [Product!]!
}

type Review {
  id: ID!
  rating: Int!
  comment: String
  author: User!
}
Enums: Enums define a fixed set of allowed values, providing type safety and self-documentation. They are ideal for status fields, categories, roles, and any field with a constrained set of options.
Interfaces: Interfaces define common fields that multiple object types must implement. They enable polymorphic queries where a field can return different object types sharing the same base interface.

Fields: Clients specify exactly which fields to retrieve, enabling efficient data fetching. Fields can be nested to traverse relationships, and aliases allow requesting the same field with different arguments.
Arguments: Every field can accept arguments for filtering, sorting, or formatting. Arguments are strongly typed and can be required or optional with default values, enabling precise data retrieval.
Aliases: Aliases let you rename the result of a field to avoid naming conflicts when requesting the same field multiple times. They are essential for comparing data or fetching multiple resources in one query.
Fragments: Fragments are reusable units of field selections that reduce duplication in queries. They can spread across multiple query operations and support conditional inclusion with `... on Type` for union/interface types.

Input Types: Input types encapsulate mutation arguments as structured objects, enabling complex nested data inputs. They are defined with the `input` keyword and support required fields, defaults, and nested input types.
Return Types: Mutations return modified or created objects to allow clients to update their local state immediately. Returning the full object is a best practice, and error information can be included via union types.
Error Handling: GraphQL returns errors in a standardized `errors` array alongside partial data. Structured error handling with error codes, field-level validation, and union types provides better client diagnostics.

Root Resolver: Root resolvers are functions that resolve each field in the Query and Mutation types. They receive four arguments: parent, args, context, and info, and can perform any async operation.
DataLoader: DataLoader batches and caches database queries to solve the N+1 problem in GraphQL. It coalesces individual requests within a single event-loop tick into a single batched query.
Batching: Batching extends DataLoader to group multiple similar operations. It's especially useful for external API calls, database queries, and compute-intensive operations where combining requests improves performance.

WebSocket: GraphQL subscriptions enable real-time communication over WebSockets. The `graphql-ws` library handles the WebSocket protocol, allowing clients to subscribe to events and receive push updates.
Event-based: Subscriptions use an async iterator pattern with a publish-subscribe mechanism. Events are triggered by mutations or external sources, and the PubSub system broadcasts data to all active subscribers.
Real-time: Real-time features like live chat, notifications, collaborative editing, and live dashboards are powered by subscriptions. Filtering, authentication, and connection management are critical for production use.

Apollo Server: Apollo Server is a production-ready GraphQL server that integrates with Express, Fastify, Lambda, and other frameworks. It provides schema stitching, caching, error handling, and Apollo Studio integration out of the box.
Apollo Client: Apollo Client manages GraphQL state on the client side, handling caching, loading states, optimistic updates, and error handling. It works with React, Vue, Angular, and plain JavaScript applications.
Cache: Apollo's InMemoryCache normalizes data by type and ID, allowing automatic deduplication and cache updates after mutations. Policies like `cache-first`, `network-only`, and `cache-and-network` control fetch behavior for optimal UX.

Apollo Federation: Apollo Federation composes multiple GraphQL services into a single schema. Each service is a subgraph with its own schema and resolvers. The gateway (Apollo Router/Rust-based) stitches them together. Federation 2 uses @key, @requires, @provides, and @shareable directives. Entities are types with a @key that can be resolved across services. @external marks fields defined elsewhere. Supergraph schema is the composed result. Rover CLI manages schema composition. Managed federation pushes schema from Apollo Studio.
GraphQL Performance & Security: GraphQL performance optimization: DataLoader batches and caches database queries (N+1 problem). dataloader library coalesces individual loads into batch requests. Query depth limiting prevents deeply nested malicious queries. Query cost analysis assigns weights to fields, rejects expensive queries. Persisted queries (APQ) allow only pre-registered queries. Rate limiting per API key. Secure: validate complex queries, mask internal errors, use allow-lists for production. graphql-query-complexity for cost analysis. graphql-depth-limit for depth limiting.
